blocks.title: The Iterator trait

blocks.explain: `v1_iter` must be `mut`: `next` changes the iterator's internal position. The `for` loop did not need that because it takes ownership of the iterator and makes it mutable behind the scenes.

blocks.title: Three ways to iterate a collection
rows: `&mut T`, to change elements in place

blocks.title: Consuming adapters
blocks.md: Methods that call `next` until the end are **consuming adapters**: they use up the iterator and produce a final value.

blocks.explain: `fold` is the general one: it starts with an accumulator and combines each item into it; `sum` and `count` are special cases. Notice the patterns `|&x|` and `|&&x|`: `iter()` yields `&i32`, and `find` passes a reference to that, so destructuring removes the layers of `&`.

blocks.title: Iterator adapters
blocks.md: **Iterator adapters** take an iterator and return a new one that changes the items somehow. Because iterators are lazy, adapters do nothing on their own; you need a consuming adapter at the end. The compiler warns you otherwise:

blocks.code:
warning: unused `Map` that must be used
 --> src/main.rs:3:5
  |
3 |     v1.iter().map(|x| x + 1);
  |     ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
  |
  = note: iterators are lazy and do nothing unless consumed
  = note: `#[warn(unused_must_use)]` (part of `#[warn(unused)]`) on by default
help: use `let _ = ...` to ignore the resulting value
  |
3 |     let _ = v1.iter().map(|x| x + 1);
  |     +++++++
blocks.explain: Add `.collect()` (with a type, such as `Vec<_>`) to run the map and gather the results.

blocks.title: Common adapters
rows: pairs each item with its index
first n / all but the first n
lets you look at the next item without consuming it

blocks.explain: Read a chain top to bottom as a pipeline. `collect` can build a `Vec`, a `String`, a `HashMap` (from pairs) and more, decided by the type you ask for; this works through the `FromIterator` trait.

steps.title: Building the chain does nothing
steps.md: `(1..=4).map(f).filter(p)` creates nested structs: a `Filter` holding a `Map` holding a `Range`. No closure has run.

steps.title: The consumer pulls the first item
steps.md: `collect` calls `next` on `Filter`, which calls `next` on `Map`, which calls `next` on the range. `1` flows up: `map 1` prints, `10` fails the filter, so `Filter` asks again.
steps.code:
map 1      // 10 rejected
map 2      // 20 kept → first item

steps.title: One item at a time, all the way through
steps.md: Each item goes through the whole pipeline before the next one starts. There are no intermediate vectors, which is why chains are cheap.

steps.title: Early exit is free
steps.md: With `.take(1)` instead of `collect`ing everything, the pipeline stops after `map 2`: items 3 and 4 are never computed.

blocks.title: Closures that capture their environment
blocks.md: Adapters take closures, and closures can capture. *The Rust Programming Language* filters shoes by the size the customer wears:

blocks.explain: The closure captures `shoe_size`. `into_iter` takes ownership of the vector, so the returned shoes are moved, not cloned.

blocks.title: Your own iterator
blocks.md: Implement `Iterator` by writing `next`, and you get every adapter for free. *Programming Rust*'s advice: if your type is a collection, also implement `IntoIterator` (often by returning a standard iterator), so it works in `for` loops.

blocks.explain: The `?` on `checked_add` ends the sequence instead of overflowing: an infinite-looking iterator that stops when the numbers would not fit. `take_while` stops the second chain long before that.

blocks.title: Loops to chains
blocks.md: Rewrite each loop in `main` as a single iterator chain. The output must not change. Try `filter`, `map`, `sum`, `max_by_key`, `enumerate` and `collect`.
blocks.task: Keep the output the same (`["ALICE", "CAROL"]`, `7`, `Some("carol")`) with no `for` loops left.

blocks.title: Iterator workout
blocks.goal: Solve data problems with iterator chains, and implement Iterator for your own type.
blocks.behavior:
Write each function as an iterator chain (loops are allowed but the point is to practise adapters):
- `pub fn word_lengths(text: &str) -> Vec<(String, usize)>`: each whitespace-separated word, lowercased, with its length in characters.
- `pub fn top_n(scores: &[(String, u32)], n: usize) -> Vec<String>`: the names of the `n` highest scores, highest first; equal scores keep their original order.
- `pub fn running_total(values: &[i64]) -> Vec<i64>`: prefix sums (`[1, 2, 3]` gives `[1, 3, 6]`). Hint: `scan`.
- `pub fn parse_all(items: &[&str]) -> Result<Vec<i32>, std::num::ParseIntError>`: parse every item, stopping at the first error. Hint: `collect` into a `Result`.
- `pub struct Collatz { n: u64, done: bool }`, created by `pub fn collatz(start: u64) -> Collatz`, iterating the Collatz sequence from `start` down to and including 1 (n even: n/2, odd: 3n+1). `collatz(6)` yields 6, 3, 10, 5, 16, 8, 4, 2, 1.
hints: `text.split_whitespace().map(|w| { let w = w.to_lowercase(); let n = w.chars().count(); (w, n) }).collect()`
`top_n`: collect references into a Vec, `sort_by(|a, b| b.1.cmp(&a.1))` (sort is stable), then `.iter().take(n).map(|s| s.0.clone()).collect()`.
`items.iter().map(|s| s.parse::<i32>()).collect()`: collecting an iterator of `Result`s into `Result<Vec<_>, _>` stops at the first `Err`.
Collatz `next`: if `done`, return `None`; remember the current `n`; if it is 1, set `done`; otherwise compute the next `n`. Return the remembered value.
blocks.solution_explain: `collect` into `Result<Vec<_>, _>` is a standard trick: it stops at the first error and returns it. `scan` is like `fold` but yields every intermediate state. `sort_by` is stable, so equal scores keep their input order, and sorting references avoids cloning names until the end.

points: Iterators are lazy; nothing happens until a consumer calls `next`.
Consumers (`sum`, `count`, `fold`, `collect`, `find`, `any`) produce a final value; adapters (`map`, `filter`, `zip`, `enumerate`, `take`...) produce new iterators.
`collect` builds whatever collection you ask for, including `Result<Vec<_>, _>`.
Implement `next` for your type and every adapter works on it.

terms.def: A value that yields a sequence of items through its next method.
Doing no work until the result is needed; iterator adapters run only when consumed.
A method like map or filter that turns one iterator into another.
A method like sum or collect that calls next until the end and produces a value.
A consumer that builds a collection (Vec, String, HashMap, Result<Vec>...) from an iterator, chosen by the target type.
